intro: Storefronts everywhere bear the names of their owners. On my daily walk to the train, I pass Dave’s Fresh Pasta, Anne Marie’s Salon, and Nellie’s Flowers.
An eponymous store name evokes familiarity, suggesting passersby are on a first-name basis with the neighborly baker, mechanic, or stylist behind it.

But there’s more to it: A store name signals authority and trustworthiness, and eponyms are no exception. Research shows first names carry connotations about age, socio-economic status, ethnicity, and a variety of personal qualities like intelligence, confidence, and honesty.
Our expectations of names are on display on the awnings and signboards all around us.

I analyzed more than 580,000 eponymns from a dataset of U.S. storefronts open at any point since 2004. To find names, I looked for words preceding an apostrophe-s and took steps to validate and deduplicate the data and account for several special cases, like when a name is referring to its location.
The result underlines the specificity of our perceptions about who sells what.
gender: For one, we have granular expectations when it comes to gender.

In some cases, the gender breakdown follows—or exaggerates—stereotypes. 



 
For example, both categories related to caretaking are among the most female.
Meanwhile, categories associated with physical labor are overwhelmingly male.
Compare garden centers to florists, which use female names 70 percent of the time.
However, despite the traditional association between women and cooking, nearly 70 percent of restaurant eponymns are male.
And the kind of dining establishment matters: pizzerias, bars, and delis are relatively likelier to use male names...
... while diners, cafes, and bakeries are relatively likelier to use female names.
Furniture stores mostly use male names, while antique and vintage stores mostly use female names.
street: Noah is by far the most popular name on daycares, commonly referencing Noah's Ark.
For a tattoo, chances are you're headed to Charlie's, Lou's, or—if you're Lucky—Lucky's.
We can see the names used most frequently for cultural cuisines, like Chinese restaurants,
Kim is the most common name on hair and nail salons. However, given the counts of Lee and Le, Kim might be a last name on nail salons more often than on hair salons.
The top auto mechanic names are all among the most common names overall.

But smaller names often have stronger ties to a business category. To see this, let's look at the names with the highest share of auto shops. Of all Conrad's, 41.6 percent are mechanics. That's more than any other name.
These associations often relate thematically.\n\n For example, Faye, April, Lilly, and Lily are among the most overrepresented on florists
Likewise, Diva has the strongest association to hair salons.
Noah and Kitty are among the most overrepresented on pet shops.\n\n Notably, eight other names are even more strongly associated with pet shops than Kitty.",
On home improvement services—plumbing, landscaping, construction, and on—several of the most overrepresented names are last names, seeming to project professionalism over warmth.
On the other hand, Troy conjures a fairly vivid image of the man coming to fix your flooring.
Sometimes, one name stands apart. \n\n Sun appears on laundry services at twice the frequency of Han, the second-most overrepresented name.
Before, we saw Le was the fourth-most common name on nail salons. \n\n A quarter of Le's are nail salons—that's a far greater share than any other name.
